title: Writers who misunderstand Afro-Cuban arranging
summary: Most Latin arrangers ignore the bass foundation, which makes his band sound different.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

Well, you were saying that with Parker (phonetic) that you felt that the best album was the one that had Mungo Manguale (phonetic) and the others.
He was a (inaudible). He was a (inaudible). He was himself.

Well, you know, what I'm getting at is then it became -- then people started writing suites. Chico wrote suites. Gil Fuller (phonetic), I think, also. And you have the time when you were from about "Afro-Jazz Suite", then you had Afro-Cuban suites and --

See, that's when -- we lose the boat. I had this here problem with Heavy Man (phonetic). Heavy Man, he wrote -- he (inaudible) he knew already. So he wrote some things for his recording. It brought -- he brought -- he had

the same problem. You don't say Afro-Cuban just to use the name (inaudible). You like to know (inaudible). And if you didn't know (inaudible) you lost. And they feel that really you just -- is on the bongos. The rhythm go and the part and the (inaudible) bass player. You've got to be able to know how to (inaudible) how to write your name in that particular number, in that particular (inaudible), and none of them ever learned that.

(inaudible) the 95 percent (inaudible) Latin arrangement in New York don't know how to write (inaudible). They put one set of bass or put a signal like American music for the bass player to (inaudible) whatever he want in that. The biggest mistake (inaudible), and they -- all they will say -- and they were asking why Machito band sound different. Oh, that's a secret, because when I make arrangement of a number, I look for the rhythm part and the bass (inaudible) used to the number first.

Like you go in and (inaudible) and get the bottom before you put the building on the top. And they don't worry about the bass. They write everything on the top, and the bottom think anybody can put anything, and that's when there be conflict of the thing. The problem, the use of the name, the Afro-Cuban, (inaudible), and then you hear the band with the conga and you (inaudible) cannot play. They even cannot function. much go on the top, and the bass is the thing (inaudible) they only that they got to stimulate (inaudible) and the piano (inaudible). So really, play something else all you hear (inaudible). Don't mean nothing. I'm glad you brought that point.

I notice very much in -- that was one of the things I noticed with the kind of fringe things I was talking about with that, for instance, when -- well, a lot of different people, jazz men playing, and they add a congo or they add a congo or bongo, and the bass player has no idea of playing timbales (phonetic). And it seems to me it was nothing for the percussion to hang on to. They literally bounce off the bass.

That's it. That's it. That's exactly, exactly what I say, exactly what I say. That is this whole mystery, exactly what I say. The best arrangement (inaudible) to ever come to nowhere, Latin one (inaudible), and nobody come over (inaudible). I say (inaudible). But his music sound completely different from anybody else. You want to know why? Because he know what's supposed to be known.

What kind of foundation he put before he start thinking about what, how many (inaudible)? And everybody think (inaudible), you put a bongo down there, play whatever you want there. That (inaudible). Chico had the same problem. He don't know that. He don't (inaudible).
